title: Long Division with Two-Digit Divisors
seo_title: Grade 5 Long Division with 2-Digit Divisors Worksheets: Estimating, Adjusting the Quotient, Remainders and Word Problems
domain: Number and Operations in Base Ten
standard_text: Find whole-number quotients of whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.
meta_desc: Free Grade 5 worksheets on dividing by 2-digit numbers: divide with multiples of 10, estimate with compatible numbers, adjust the quotient digit, long division and area models with 4-digit dividends, zeros in the quotient, remainders and word problems. 100 practice questions with step-by-step answers.
key_big: Round the divisor to estimate each digit. Then check: too big, try one less; remainder too big, try one more.
key_sub: Use compatible numbers (312 ÷ 41 is about 320 ÷ 40 = 8). The remainder must be less than the divisor, and every digit you bring down needs a digit in the quotient, even 0. Check: quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend.
body_html:
The big idea

Dividing by a two-digit number uses the same four steps as before: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down. The new part is the divide step. You cannot just know 238 ÷ 48 as a fact, so you estimate, try a digit and fix it if needed.

Estimate with compatible numbers

Round the divisor to the nearest ten. Then change the dividend to a nearby number that divides easily.

Example

Estimate 312 ÷ 41.

41 is close to 40. 320 is close to 312, and 32 ÷ 4 = 8, so 320 ÷ 40 = 8.

Answer: about 8 (exactly 7 R 25)

Multiples of 10 work like basic facts: cross out the same number of zeros in both numbers. 3,600 ÷ 40 = 360 ÷ 4 = 90.

Long division with a two-digit divisor

Adjust the estimate

Rounding the divisor can make a try one too big or one too small. Look at what you get:

What you seeWhat it meansFix
The product is more than the numberThe digit is too bigTry one less
The difference is the divisor or moreThe digit is too smallTry one more
Example

182 ÷ 26

Round 26 to 30: 182 ÷ 30 is about 6. 6 × 26 = 156 and 182 − 156 = 26. 26 is not less than 26, so 6 is too small. Try 7: 7 × 26 = 182.

Answer: 7

Another way: area model and partial quotients

Take away easy chunks of the divisor (× 10, × 50, …) until nothing is left. Then add the chunks.

Remainders and checking

The remainder is always less than the divisor. If the divisor does not fit after you bring down, write 0 in the quotient.

Check every answer: quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend. 200 × 27 + 12 = 5,412.

Word problems: what does the remainder mean?

The question asksUse the remainder like this500 students, 48 on each bus: 500 ÷ 48 = 10 R 20
How many are needed for everyone?Add 1 to the quotient11 buses
How many full groups?Leave the remainder out10 full buses
How many are left over?The remainder is the answer20 students

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Keeping a try that is too small (182 ÷ 26 = 6 R 26)If the difference is the divisor or more, add 1 to the digit
Skipping a zero (5,412 ÷ 27 = 20 R 12)Every digit you bring down needs a digit in the quotient
Crossing out different numbers of zeros (3,600 ÷ 40 = 9)Cross out the same number of zeros: 360 ÷ 4 = 90
Ignoring the remainder in a word problemAsk: do the leftovers need one more bus, box or row?

faq.q: How do you divide by a two-digit number?
faq.a: Use long division: estimate how many times the divisor fits by rounding it to the nearest ten, multiply, subtract and bring down the next digit. Repeat until every digit is used.

faq.q: What do you do when your estimate in long division is wrong?
faq.a: If the product is bigger than the number you are dividing, try one less. If the difference is equal to or more than the divisor, try one more.

faq.q: How do you check a long division answer with a remainder?
faq.a: Multiply the quotient by the divisor and add the remainder. For 2,385 ÷ 48 = 49 R 33: 49 × 48 + 33 = 2,385.
It is the Common Core Grade 5 standard for dividing whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends by two-digit divisors, and explaining the work with equations, arrays or area models.

sets.title: Divide with multiples of 10 and estimate

items.q: What is 450 ÷ 90?
items.e: Cross out one zero in each number: 450 ÷ 90 = 45 ÷ 9. 45 ÷ 9 = 5. Check: 5 × 90 = 450.

items.q: What is 630 ÷ 70?
items.e: Cross out one zero in each number: 630 ÷ 70 = 63 ÷ 7. 63 ÷ 7 = 9. Check: 9 × 70 = 630.

items.q: What is 180 ÷ 90?
items.e: Cross out one zero in each number: 180 ÷ 90 = 18 ÷ 9. 18 ÷ 9 = 2. Check: 2 × 90 = 180.

items.q: What is 140 ÷ 70?
items.e: Cross out one zero in each number: 140 ÷ 70 = 14 ÷ 7. 14 ÷ 7 = 2. Check: 2 × 70 = 140.

items.q: What is 1,800 ÷ 60?
items.e: Cross out one zero in each number: 1,800 ÷ 60 = 180 ÷ 6. 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so 180 ÷ 6 = 30. Be careful: cross out the same number of zeros in both numbers. Check: 30 × 60 = 1,800.

items.q: What is 5,400 ÷ 60?
items.e: Cross out one zero in each number: 5,400 ÷ 60 = 540 ÷ 6. 54 ÷ 6 = 9, so 540 ÷ 6 = 90. Be careful: cross out the same number of zeros in both numbers. Check: 90 × 60 = 5,400.

items.q: What is 2,000 ÷ 40?
items.e: Cross out one zero in each number: 2,000 ÷ 40 = 200 ÷ 4. 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so 200 ÷ 4 = 50. Be careful: 2,000 has 3 zeros, but one of them belongs to the fact 20 ÷ 4. Check: 50 × 40 = 2,000.

items.q: What number goes in the box? ☐ × 80 = 5,600
items.e: Think: what number times 80 is 5,600? That is 5,600 ÷ 80 = 560 ÷ 8 = 70. Check: 70 × 80 = 5,600.

items.q: What number goes in the box? ☐ × 30 = 240
items.e: Think: what number times 30 is 240? That is 240 ÷ 30 = 24 ÷ 3 = 8. Check: 8 × 30 = 240.

items.q: What number goes in the box? ☐ × 40 = 3,600
items.e: Think: what number times 40 is 3,600? That is 3,600 ÷ 40 = 360 ÷ 4 = 90. Check: 90 × 40 = 3,600.

items.q: Use compatible numbers to estimate 142 ÷ 27.
items.e: Round 27 to 30. A number close to 142 that 30 divides easily is 150, because 15 ÷ 3 = 5. 150 ÷ 30 = 5, so 142 ÷ 27 is about 5. (The exact answer is 5 R 7, which is close.)

items.q: Use compatible numbers to estimate 621 ÷ 93.
items.e: Round 93 to 90. A number close to 621 that 90 divides easily is 630, because 63 ÷ 9 = 7. 630 ÷ 90 = 7, so 621 ÷ 93 is about 7. (The exact answer is 6 R 63, which is close.)

items.q: Use compatible numbers to estimate 553 ÷ 79.
items.e: Round 79 to 80. A number close to 553 that 80 divides easily is 560, because 56 ÷ 8 = 7. 560 ÷ 80 = 7, so 553 ÷ 79 is about 7. (The exact answer is 7, which is close.)

items.q: Use compatible numbers to estimate 1,015 ÷ 48.
items.e: Round 48 to 50. A number close to 1,015 that 50 divides easily is 1,000, because 10 ÷ 5 = 2. 1,000 ÷ 50 = 20, so 1,015 ÷ 48 is about 20. (The exact answer is 21 R 7, which is close.)

items.q: Use compatible numbers to estimate 4,219 ÷ 61.
items.e: Round 61 to 60. A number close to 4,219 that 60 divides easily is 4,200, because 42 ÷ 6 = 7. 4,200 ÷ 60 = 70, so 4,219 ÷ 61 is about 70. (The exact answer is 69 R 10, which is close.)

items.q: Use compatible numbers to estimate 2,138 ÷ 73.
items.e: Round 73 to 70. A number close to 2,138 that 70 divides easily is 2,100, because 21 ÷ 7 = 3. 2,100 ÷ 70 = 30, so 2,138 ÷ 73 is about 30. (The exact answer is 29 R 21, which is close.)

items.q: Which numbers are best for estimating 311 ÷ 44?
items.e: Round 44 to 40. Then find a number near 311 that 40 divides easily: 32 ÷ 4 = 8, so use 320 ÷ 40 = 8. 300 ÷ 40 and 310 ÷ 40 do not come out evenly.

items.q: Which numbers are best for estimating 458 ÷ 93?
items.e: Round 93 to 90. Then find a number near 458 that 90 divides easily: 45 ÷ 9 = 5, so use 450 ÷ 90 = 5. 460 ÷ 90 and 500 ÷ 90 do not come out evenly.

items.q: Which numbers are best for estimating 204 ÷ 29?
items.e: Round 29 to 30. Then find a number near 204 that 30 divides easily: 21 ÷ 3 = 7, so use 210 ÷ 30 = 7. 200 ÷ 30 does not come out evenly.

items.q: Which numbers are best for estimating 801 ÷ 93?
items.e: Round 93 to 90. Then find a number near 801 that 90 divides easily: 81 ÷ 9 = 9, so use 810 ÷ 90 = 9. 800 ÷ 90 does not come out evenly.

items.q: Omar divides 395 ÷ 44. He rounds 44 to 40 and tries 9. 9 × 44 = 396, which is more than 395. What should he do next?
items.e: 396 is more than 395, so 9 is too big. Try 8: 8 × 44 = 352 and 395 − 352 = 43, which is less than 44. So 395 ÷ 44 = 8 R 43. Check: 8 × 44 + 43 = 395.

items.q: What is 340 ÷ 68?
items.e: Round 68 to 70. 340 ÷ 70 is about 4, so try 4. 4 × 68 = 272 and 340 − 272 = 68, which is not less than 68, so 4 is too small. Try 5. 5 × 68 = 340 and 340 − 340 = 0. Answer: 5. Check: 5 × 68 = 340.

items.q: What is the remainder when 111 is divided by 18?
items.e: The question asks for the remainder, not the quotient. Round 18 to 20. 111 ÷ 20 is about 5, so try 5. 5 × 18 = 90 and 111 − 90 = 21, which is not less than 18, so 5 is too small. Try 6. 6 × 18 = 108 and 111 − 108 = 3. Answer: 6 R 3. Check: 6 × 18 + 3 = 111.

items.q: What is the remainder when 259 is divided by 64?

items.q: What is 112 ÷ 14?

items.q: To divide 254 ÷ 45, which product should you use?
items.e: You need the greatest product that is not more than 254. 6 × 45 = 270 is too big, and 5 × 45 = 225 leaves 29, which is less than 45. So 254 ÷ 45 = 5 R 29.

items.e: 39 is less than 83, so the quotient has no hundreds. Start with 395 tens. 3,953 ÷ 83 = 47 R 52, which has 2 digits.

items.q: Divide.
items.e: 5 is less than 25, so start with 52. 52 ÷ 25 = 2: 2 × 25 = 50, 52 − 50 = 2. Bring down 0: 25 does not fit into 20, so write 0 in the quotient. Bring down 0: 200 ÷ 25 = 8: 8 × 25 = 200, 200 − 200 = 0. Answer: 208. Check: 208 × 25 = 5,200.

items.e: Dividend = quotient × divisor + remainder: 56 × 34 = 1,904, 1,904 + 12 = 1,916. Check: 1,916 ÷ 34 = 56 R 12.

sets.title: Word problems: what to do with the remainder

items.q: A bakery is delivering 647 muffins. Each tray holds 18 muffins. How many trays are needed for all the muffins?
items.e: Divide: 6 is less than 18, so start with 64. 64 ÷ 18 = 3: 3 × 18 = 54, 64 − 54 = 10. Bring down 7: 107 ÷ 18 = 5: 5 × 18 = 90, 107 − 90 = 17. Nothing is left to bring down, so the remainder is 17. So 647 ÷ 18 = 35 R 17. Check: 35 × 18 + 17 = 647. 35 trays are not enough: 17 muffins still need a tray. Add 1 more, so the answer is 36 trays.

items.q: A farm collected 1,565 eggs. It packs them in cartons of 12. How many cartons can it fill completely?
items.e: Divide: 1 is less than 12, so start with 15. 15 ÷ 12 = 1: 1 × 12 = 12, 15 − 12 = 3. Bring down 6: 36 ÷ 12 = 3: 3 × 12 = 36, 36 − 36 = 0. Bring down 5: 12 does not fit into 5, so write 0 in the quotient. Nothing is left to bring down, so the remainder is 5. So 1,565 ÷ 12 = 130 R 5. Check: 130 × 12 + 5 = 1,565. The 5 eggs left over are not enough to fill another carton, so leave the remainder out. The answer is 130 cartons.

items.q: A school raised $1,965 at a fun fair. It shares the money equally among 15 classes. How much money does each class get?
items.e: Divide: 1 is less than 15, so start with 19. 19 ÷ 15 = 1: 1 × 15 = 15, 19 − 15 = 4. Bring down 6: 46 ÷ 15 = 3: 3 × 15 = 45, 46 − 45 = 1. Bring down 5: 15 ÷ 15 = 1: 1 × 15 = 15, 15 − 15 = 0. So 1,965 ÷ 15 = 131. Check: 131 × 15 = 1,965. There is no remainder, so the answer is $131.

items.q: Grace has $305 saved. Concert tickets cost $28 each. How many tickets can she buy?
items.e: Divide: 3 is less than 28, so start with 30. 30 ÷ 28 = 1: 1 × 28 = 28, 30 − 28 = 2. Bring down 5: 28 does not fit into 25, so write 0 in the quotient. Nothing is left to bring down, so the remainder is 25. So 305 ÷ 28 = 10 R 25. Check: 10 × 28 + 25 = 305. The 25 dollars left over are not enough to buy another ticket, so leave the remainder out. The answer is 10 tickets.
